{"id":"persona-vvs2","title":"Windows support: the transport abstraction is the gate","description":"README:84 promises a Windows named pipe at \\.\pipe\persona-workload-{sid}, README:90 promises EXE-signing consumer attestation, and the attestor table lists Windows for Tailscale, FIDO2 and Windows Hello. None of it exists, there is no Windows CI leg, and the code is structurally Unix-only.

Measured on this tree:
  21 sites   UnixListener / UnixStream        -> named pipes
   4 sites   libc::getuid                     -> SID
   4 sites   SO_PEERCRED                      -> GetNamedPipeClientProcessId
   1 site    tokio::signal::unix              -> ctrl_c or service control handler
   2 files   tailscale.rs, ssh.rs assume unix sockets
Exactly one #[cfg(not(unix))] exists in the whole workspace.

The 21 transport sites are the gate. Nothing else can be attempted until the listener and stream are an abstraction rather than a concrete tokio::net::Unix* type, because the socket path, consumer attestation and the daemon's accept loop all bottom out there. persona-grpc/src/socket.rs already carries the ponytail comment saying so: 'unix domain sockets only | ceiling: Windows needs a named pipe, which this function cannot express | upgrade path: abstract the transport over UnixListener/UnixStream first, then return a platform-tagged endpoint instead of a PathBuf'.

The good news, and where to start: persona-core is ALREADY portable. Zero files reference std::os::unix, libc, or unix sockets, and its dependencies (thiserror, serde, hkdf, sha2, ring, x509-cert, jsonwebtoken, serde_json) all build on Windows. That crate holds the crypto, the HKDF pseudonym derivation, the SPIFFE ID types and the signer.

Suggested order:
  1. Windows CI leg for persona-core only, to lock in the portability that exists.
  2. Abstract the transport.
  3. Then named pipe path, Windows consumer attestation, signal handling.
  4. Then decide whether Windows Hello is an attestor worth writing.","status":"open","priority":2,"issue_type":"epic","owner":"mark@reviewcommit.com","created_at":"2026-09-14T05:14:38.067052385Z","created_by":"agent","updated_at":"2026-09-14T05:14:38.067052385Z","labels":["windows","portability"]}

{"notes":"SCOPE NARROWED 2026-09-15 (commit 34cab94), after Mark asked whether we were over-specifying Windows. We were, and one piece was already frozen.

REMOVED: ConsumerIdentity::MsixPublisher and its 'msix:publisher:{cn}' selector key. That string was inside the HKDF info input, so it was a wire commitment changeable only by a scheme bump -- made for a platform with no code, by a variant nothing ever constructed. It was probably wrong too: a publisher CN is shared across every app from one publisher, so all of them would derive the same pseudonym, which is exactly the global-correlator failure attest_peer refuses to build from uid, and asymmetric with MacosBundleId (app AND publisher). No scheme bump was needed since nothing had ever derived from it.

CORRECTED: the socket was specified as \\.\pipe\hire-workload-{sid}, which we invented. SPIRE binds its Workload API at \spire-agent\public\api with NO SID in the name, isolating per user by DACL. The spec now says \\.\pipe\hired\public\api and names whose convention that is. 'hired invents no protocol' applies to the endpoint convention too.

WHAT THIS EPIC SHOULD NOT DO: re-add a Windows ConsumerIdentity variant, or re-specify a pipe name, ahead of the code. Whoever implements Windows consumer attestation picks the identity then, knowing what the platform offers -- Authenticode thumbprint, package family name, or something else -- and defends the format at that point.

STILL ACCURATE: the transport is the gate. Measurement refreshed today: 35 UnixListener/UnixStream sites (the bead says 21; it predates bind_listener and the flock work). WAM, GetNamedPipeClientProcessId and Windows Hello remain research notes here, deliberately NOT promises in the spec -- the platform tables now mark all of them (not implemented)."}
